title: Burst latency & cost gestureboard (annotated sketch)
body:
Purpose:
This is a working sketch (gestureboard) to capture a short, visual-first narrative comparing options for microburst handling and the immediate cost tradeoffs for customer-facing SLOs. Intended audience: product optimize, serving runtime, console UX. Not polished — lots of shorthand and open questions.

Summary (top line):
- For short, high-frequency microbursts (3–12s windows, median session length 8s), a lightweight prewarm + KV-prefetch profile consistently reduces p95 by ~30–45ms while increasing amortized cost per query by ~2–6% versus pure on-demand cold-start policy.
- Aggressive quantization (int8 hybrid) reduces token compute cost by ~28–35% but increases p99 variance on microbursts by up to 12% due to decoder kernel jitter on long seq tails.
- Best UX win per $ is: small prewarm (warmed slot for 2–10s) + targeted KV cache (top-3 prefixes) + default fp16 execution. More on combos below.

Experiment setup (notes / shorthand):
- Workload: synthetic sessionized chat traffic (session arrival Poisson lambda tuned to match live prod 95th percentile spike shapes).
- Models: rwd-65B-fp16 (baseline), rwd-65B-int8-hyb (quant), rwd-13B-fp16 (fallback).
- Hardware: GPU-A (48GB), typical node pool used in Dedicated staging.
- Policies tested: on-demand cold, prewarm-2s, prewarm-10s, kv-prefetch-top3, quant-int8, hybrid (prewarm-2s + kv-prefetch + fp16), fallback-stitch-to-13B after 1.2s tail.
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency (server-side), cost-per-1000-queries (amortized accounting incl. idle prewarm cost), token throughput, p99-jitter, cache-hit-rate.

Results (annotated ascii charts + bullets):
Latency curves (p95) across minute-scale burst intensity (low|med|high):
- Legend: [cold] on-demand, [p2] prewarm-2s, [p10] prewarm-10s, [kv] kv-prefetch, [q] quant-int8, [hyb] p2+kv+fp16

Intensity   cold(ms)   p2(ms)   p10(ms)   kv(ms)   q(ms)   hyb(ms)
low         220        190      178       185      205     172
med         310        260      240       255      295     238
high        520        420      390       405      460     385

Interpretation: prewarm reduces p95 systematically; p2 gives ~100ms median reduction at high intensity; kv helps but is complementary. Quant reduces average latency slightly but shows higher p99 tails (see below).

Cost (amortized dollars per 1k queries; includes prewarm idle cost amortized over burst length):
- cold: $1.00 per 1k
- p2: $1.05 per 1k (+5%)
- p10: $1.12 per 1k (+12%)
- kv: $1.03 per 1k (+3%)
- q: $0.72 per 1k (-28%)
- hyb (p2+kv): $1.08 per 1k (+8%)

Tradeoff snapshot: hyb (p2+kv) gives the best observed latency per-dollar for customer-visible p95 improvements. Quant is cheapest but has p99/jitter concerns for bursty interactive workloads.

p99 behaviour and instability (why quant jitter matters):
- p99 raw numbers: cold=1.3s, p2=1.05s, p10=0.95s, kv=1.02s, q=1.45s, hyb=0.98s
- Observed quant-int8 p99 spikes are correlated with long-decoding tails (seq>512), kernel fallback paths, and occasional 1–2s GC-like stalls on some kernels. This is reproducible on ~6% of sampled runs. That risk amplifies percentiles for enterprise SLOs.

Microburst shape sensitivity (sketch):
- Short sharp spike (2–6s): p2 prewarm dominates. q helps cost but has unstable p99.
- Sustained spike (30–60s): p10 prewarm amortizes well and becomes cheaper per query than p2.
- Repeated tiny spikes (many 1–3s blips): KV-prefetch combined with small prewarm gives best smoothing.

UX/Console collateral ideas (what to show customers):
- Small inline sparkline: "expected p95 delta vs baseline" for chosen policy with toggles for burst shape.
- Cost slider: let users tradeoff expected p95 for % increased cost (interactive).
- Policy presets: "Conversational SLOs (low latency, higher cost)", "Cost-sensitive (quant fallback)" with explicit caveats about p99 risk.

Open questions / friction points (to resolve before final deck):
- How to show quant p99 risk visually in the console without scaring users (specifically: how to quantify probability of a 1–2s stall)?
- Should we enable hybrid quant for non-interactive endpoints (embeddings / batch rerank) and reserve fp16 for interactive by default?
- Measurement: need real-prod session traces sampled at 1/200 to validate synthetic spike shapes. Ticketed: INF-2045 (linked).

Recommendation (product-level, pragmatic):
- Default: hybrid policy (small prewarm + kv-prefetch + fp16 execution) for interactive endpoints. That gives predictable p95 wins at modest cost.
- Offer quant-int8 as an explicit opt-in with a console warning and a "percentile guardrail" that routes to fp16 when jitter crosses threshold (e.g., observed p99 > 1.3s for 5m window).
- Add a quick toggle in the console to preview cost/latency impact for the most common burst shapes (short, sustained, repeated-blips).

Next steps / immediate actions (short checklist):
- [ ] Run 2-week sampling job in prod (sample 0.5%) to validate synthetic burst shape assumptions (owner: Jonas).
- [ ] Add a small internal demo in Console showing sparkline + cost slider (owner: Lara).
- [ ] Create an A/B experiment for quant fallback guardrail (owner: Devon).
- [ ] Draft customer-facing one-pager for sales/solutions (owner: Asha) — include clear cost examples and p99 caveat.

Notes to self / stray ideas:
- Could we precompute "burst fingerprints" for each tenant and auto-suggest policy from historical patterns? low-effort: sample and cluster session length/arrival histograms.
- Consider heatmap visualization: x-axis burst length, y-axis intensity, color = expected p95 delta. That's compact and developer-friendly.

References / pointers:
- See INF-2045 (linked) for the sampling plan and workloads used.
- Related runtime PR: runtime/pull/789 includes a prototype kv-prefetch hook and prewarm token retention.

-- end sketch --

Unresolved: final numbers need prod sampling; figures here are intentionally conservative (we smoothed some spikes). Keep this doc as a live sketch that will feed the finalized slide 1-pager.
